clue.text: Conservative outburst by one who's pissed with it?

blocks.note: C is the standard abbreviation for Conservative
the involuntary hiccup of a drunk person

explanation.surface: A Tory lets slip a drunken outburst, maybe from someone fashionably hip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pissed' is British slang for drunk, and a drunk's outburst is the hiccup HIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone 'with it' is fashionable and stylish, which is what chic describes.

clue.text: Means of corporal punishment has our leftie Daves arse-over-tip

indicators.note: falling arse over tip means turning head over heels, so the word is turned the other way round

blocks.note: Dave Spart is Private Eye's own ranting left-wing columnist, made plural here

explanation.surface: A tabloid jibe that the magazine's left-wingers are tumbling over amid talk of beatings.
explanation.walkthrough: Dave Spart is the Private Eye parody of a far-left activist; 'our' signals the magazine's own character. SPARTS read backwards gives STRAPS.
explanation.definitionFit: Leather straps were used for beating pupils in schools, so they are instruments of corporal punishment.

clue.text: Throw up hair-balls

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the word is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: to lob is to throw something in a high arc
locks are tresses of hair

explanation.surface: A cat coughing up a hairball, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen in 'hair-balls' welds wordplay to definition: 'hair' is LOCKS, and 'balls' is the definition. Thrown upward, LOB becomes BOL.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are British slang for testicles and, figuratively, for nonsense or rubbish talk.

clue.text: Corporation owner stuffing model in middle of heaving sofa

indicators.note: a heaving thing is tossed and churned about, so the letters are rearranged
stuffing goes inside something, so one piece is placed within the other
this names where the stuffing is placed: right in the centre of the shuffled word

blocks.note: the Ford Model T gives the letter T
taken as written

explanation.surface: A media tycoon and a model stuffed together onto a heaving sofa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' looks like a company, so 'owner' suggests a mogul; but corporation is an old jokey word for a pot belly.
explanation.definitionFit: A corporation is a paunch, so someone who has a big one is a fat person, rudely called a fatso.

clue.text: Labour on the Lords? "Defunct institution!"

indicators.note: in a down clue, one thing on another sits above it, so the first piece comes first

blocks.note: labour means toil
the House of Lords, Parliament's upper chamber

explanation.surface: A political exchange: the Labour Party's view of the House of Lords is that it is an obsolete institution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' poses as the political party but is plain work.
explanation.definitionFit: Workhouses housed the destitute in Britain until they were abolished in the twentieth century, so they are an institution no longer existing.

clue.text: Sense pathetic concealment of Condoleezza's debut bust-ups

indicators.note: something pathetic is a wreck, so its letters are put in a new order
the shuffled word conceals the next piece inside it
a debut is a first appearance, so the first letter of the name is used

blocks.note: taken as written
Condoleezza Rice, the US Secretary of State

explanation.surface: Commentary on Condoleezza Rice's pitiful attempts to hide early rows.
explanation.definitionFit: Making a scene means having a public row, so scenes are noisy quarrels or bust-ups.

clue.text: It's set to go up as Tim Rice's ultimate flop

indicators.note: ultimate means last, so only the final letter of the word is used

blocks.note: taken as written
Tim Rice the lyricist
a show that bombs is a flop

explanation.surface: Tim Rice's latest musical is headed for disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go up' sounds like a curtain rising on a show; here it means explode.
explanation.definitionFit: A time bomb is primed with a timer so it will explode at a chosen moment.

clue.text: Blair not up to a year?

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the word is read from the bottom

blocks.note: taken as written
Y is the abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: A question whether Blair is fit for another year in office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not up to' reads as a phrase meaning incapable, but 'up' turns NOT over and 'to' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Tony is the first name of former Prime Minister Blair, so the surname defines it by example.

clue.text: It could be politically embarrassing, Lancashire offering to get a Tory leader round

indicators.note: the leader of the word is its first letter

blocks.note: Lancashire hotpot is a lamb and potato stew from that county in north-west England
taken as written
the first letter of the party name
a round shape is the letter O

explanation.surface: Lancashire voters putting on a dish to win round a Conservative leader could prove awkward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Offering' suggests a political pledge, but it is a dish served up.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot potato is an idiom for a controversial issue that nobody wants to handle.

clue.text: City: "Cameron's opening broadcast ordinary"

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: David Cameron's name
to air a programme is to broadcast it
O is the abbreviation for ordinary, as in O level

explanation.surface: A review dismissing Cameron's first broadcast as ordinary, like a newspaper headline.
explanation.definitionFit: Cairo is the capital of Egypt, so it is one example of a city.

clue.text: (& 12) Ex-leader, a lush existence possibly behind him, one who would be king and US president?

definitions.text: Ex-leader, a lush existence possibly behind him

blocks.note: Prince Charles, then heir to the British throne
John F Kennedy

explanation.surface: A sketch of a former party leader who has given up drink, framed as royal and presidential ambitions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A lush existence' looks like luxury but a lush is a drunk; Charles Kennedy led the Liberal Democrats and stepped down over his drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: He was a former Liberal Democrat party leader whose alcoholism was public knowledge, hence the drinking past.

clue.text: (see 11)
Principles harked back to by vote-seeking politician, leader of Conservatives needing all-round support

definitions.text: Principles harked back to by vote-seeking politician

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter
something all round another surrounds it, so the next word goes outside the leader's letter

blocks.note: the party name
a basis is a foundation or support

explanation.surface: A campaigning politician returns to old principles while the Tory leader needs support from all sides.
explanation.walkthrough: The long definition alludes to John Major's 1993 slogan 'Back to Basics'.
explanation.definitionFit: Basics are fundamental principles, and 'back to basics' was the political slogan the definition describes.

clue.text: As one back on the Tory front bench, Nick overturns lives

definitions.text: As one back on the Tory front bench

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning something over flips the word end to end

blocks.note: to nick is to steal or rob
lives in the sense of exists

explanation.surface: A Tory returns to the front bench while someone called Nick upends lives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' poses as a person's name but is the verb to steal.
explanation.definitionFit: Boris Johnson rejoined the Conservative front bench, so he was one back on it at the time.

clue.text: Queer yob on reconnoitre for a camp type

indicators.note: queer in its old sense of odd or strange, so these letters are set out oddly

blocks.note: taken as written
to scout is to reconnoitre

explanation.surface: A cheeky line about an odd lout on a camp type's mission.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Camp' suggests flamboyance, as 'queer' does, but here it means the tents of a scouting trip.
explanation.definitionFit: Boy scouts famously go camping, so a boy scout is a type who goes to camp.

clue.text: Pissed but not lashing out

blocks.note: first meaning: drunk, in British slang
second meaning: stingy, as lashing out means spending freely

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lashing out' looks like violence from a drunk, but in British usage it means splashing out money.
explanation.definitionFit: Tight is British slang both for drunk and for mean with money, unwilling to spend freely.

clue.text: How a drink problem is a crafty thing

blocks.note: surface reading: describing the nature of alcoholism
setter's reading: drinking is work done with the hand, lifting the glass

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as hand-i-work: constant drinking is a job for the hand that raises the glass.
explanation.definitionFit: Handiwork is something made by hand, a product of craft or skill.

clue.text: (& see 21) Glenda Slagg type's messy collection?

blocks.note: first meaning: an old ... who writes for a ..., a tabloid newspaper
second meaning: a jumbled assortment

explanation.walkthrough: Glenda Slagg is Private Eye's spoof of a gushing tabloid columnist; a rag is a trashy newspaper and a bag a rude word for a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A ragbag is a miscellaneous jumble of things, and jokingly a frumpy tabloid hack.

clue.text: Dread being squeezed by a flipping Kray twin and his ilk

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the name is read backwards
squeezed by means held tightly inside the other piece

blocks.note: angst is anxious dread
Reggie Kray, one of the notorious London gangland twins

explanation.surface: A frightened man squeezed by a furious Kray twin and his crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' poses as a mild British curse, the kind an East End hard man might use, but it is the instruction to turn the name round.
explanation.definitionFit: The Krays were East End criminals, so their ilk, the kind they belong to, is the gangster.

clue.text: Sawn-off shotguns initially going to each city

indicators.note: something gone off is spoiled, so the letters are set in a new order
initially means at the start, so the first letter of the word is used

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of the word
EA is the abbreviation for each

explanation.surface: Sawn-off shotguns reaching every city, like a crime report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sawn-off' reads as one word, but the hyphen splits fodder from indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Swansea is a city on the south coast of Wales, so it is one example.

clue.text: Meeting of politicians gives you erection

blocks.note: first meaning: a legislative body such as the Welsh ...
second meaning: the act of putting something together or building it

explanation.walkthrough: The smutty reading of 'erection' is a decoy; it means construction, as in assembling a structure.
explanation.definitionFit: An assembly is a gathering of lawmakers, and also the putting together of a structure from its parts.

clue.text: (see 17)
Tabloid's hell - no point getting protection from burning!

indicators.note: having no compass point means that letter is dropped from the word

blocks.note: The Sun is a British tabloid, here with its possessive s
Hades is the underworld of Greek myth
S, south, is a compass point

explanation.surface: A tabloid's hell-raising has no point, while readers seek sunburn protection.
explanation.definitionFit: A sunshade is a parasol or awning that shields people from the sun's burning rays.

clue.text: Cripes! Foreign article put off one trying to make a speech

definitions.text: put off one trying to make a speech

blocks.note: both are mild exclamations of surprise
le is French for 'the'

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims as a foreign news piece distracts a speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put off' looks like a postponed article, but it is the verb to distract.
explanation.definitionFit: To heckle is to interrupt a speaker with jeers, which puts the speaker off their stride.

clue.text: Thumbs up Bush's arse – ten twiddles

indicators.note: to twiddle is to twist and fiddle, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: ass is the American word for arse, as George W Bush would say it
taken as written

explanation.surface: A crude image of a body part up the president's behind, and ten twiddling digits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thumbs up' looks like part of the rude picture but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A thumbs-up is a gesture of approval or agreement, which is what assent means.

clue.text: Goofs in print perpetrated by arsehole beset by age

indicators.note: beset by means surrounded on all sides, so one word sits inside the other

blocks.note: an era is an age
a rat is a contemptible person

explanation.surface: Printing blunders committed by an ageing jerk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arsehole' here is a nasty person, which a rat also is.
explanation.definitionFit: Errata are a list of misprints in a book, so they are printed mistakes.

clue.text: Very dodgy gins screw you digitally

indicators.note: something dodgy is unreliable or crooked, so the letters go astray

blocks.note: V is the abbreviation for very
taken as written

explanation.surface: Bad gin drinks leave you feeling cheated online.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digitally' suggests computers, but it means with the fingers.
explanation.definitionFit: The V-sign, made with two fingers and palm inward, is a rude British gesture meaning roughly 'get lost'.

clue.text: Bill tossed by quiet Daisy – a nice little earner

indicators.note: something tossed is flipped over, so it reads backwards

blocks.note: AC is the abbreviation for account, which a bill is
sh is the call for quiet
Daisy is a traditional name for a cow

explanation.surface: Someone called Bill is thrown aside by a quiet girl named Daisy, who is a money-maker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' and 'Daisy' look like two people; one is an account, the other a dairy animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A cash cow is a reliable source of steady profit, and 'a nice little earner' is the British idiom for one.

clue.text: Chuck's group of luvvies

blocks.note: first meaning: to throw
second meaning: the actors in a production

explanation.walkthrough: 'Chuck's' looks like someone's name with a possessive; the 's is 'is'. Luvvies is a British jibe for gushing actors.
explanation.definitionFit: Cast means to throw, and the cast of a play is its whole company of actors.

clue.text: Military type knocked back drink, like, before one-to-one

indicators.note: knocked back suggests downing a drink but here means sent backwards

blocks.note: rum is a spirit
as in the sense of like
a in the sense of one
the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A soldier downed a drink, like, before a one-to-one meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One-to-one' sounds like a private chat; it is two separate ones, A and I, with 'to' joining them.
explanation.definitionFit: A samurai was a member of Japan's hereditary warrior class, so a military type.

clue.text: This Lady Thatcher giving one to Reagan?

definitions.note: the answer fills the blank in the nickname, the Iron Lady

blocks.note: the Roman numeral one
Ronald Reagan, US president, known as Ron

explanation.surface: A saucy hint at Margaret Thatcher giving Ronald Reagan one.
explanation.walkthrough: Thatcher was nicknamed the Iron Lady, so 'This Lady' asks for the word that precedes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Margaret Thatcher was famously the Iron Lady, a nickname from a Soviet newspaper for her toughness.

clue.text: He came before 11/12, showing extreme hardness

blocks.note: first meaning: David ..., an earlier Liberal leader
second meaning: the strong alloy of iron

explanation.walkthrough: David Steel led the Liberals years before the 11/12 answer led the Liberal Democrats.
explanation.definitionFit: David Steel was a predecessor as party leader, and the alloy is a byword for toughness.

clue.text: Opera duo finally admitted to Glitter's corrupt circle

indicators.note: finally means the last letter of the word is used
admitted to means let into another piece, so it goes inside
something corrupt is debased and twisted, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: Gary Glitter, the disgraced glam-rock singer
the closing letter of the word
a circle is shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A pair let into Gary Glitter's corrupt circle, a dig at his crimes.
explanation.definitionFit: Rigoletto is Verdi's opera about a hunchbacked court jester, so it is one example.
